prose.summary: A recruiter fills open roles: sourcing candidates, running screens, chasing hiring managers for feedback, and closing offers before someone else does. In practice a lot of postings under this title in Switzerland and Germany are procurement or vendor-facing recruiting roles rather than pure HR, which is why skills like SAP and procurement show up as often as they do. The confusion people have is with HR generalist work: a recruiter owns the pipeline until someone signs, an HR manager owns them after.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split into three kinds of time: sourcing and screening (alone, on LinkedIn or an ATS), calls with candidates, and calibration meetings with hiring managers who keep changing what they want. Monday often starts with a pipeline review, going role by role to see who dropped out and why. Screens run 20 to 30 minutes and you do a handful a day when a search is live. The part people look forward to is the offer call, the one where you get to tell someone they got it and hear the pause before they say yes. Writing job ads and chasing feedback from a hiring manager who has gone quiet for a week takes up more time than anyone expects going in. The rest is scheduling, which is its own quiet skill: getting five calendars to agree on one hour.
prose.work_environment: This is desk work, mostly in an office, with the phone and video calls doing the heavy lifting instead of any lab or site. Remote share sits low at 19 percent, which tracks: hiring managers and candidates both want a recruiter reachable at short notice, and a lot of the job is reading a room on a call. Bad weeks come from hiring freezes that get announced mid-search, or from a manager who wanted five people by Friday and just added a sixth req. Travel is rare for this role unless you're recruiting across borders for a company with sites in several countries, which is common in Swiss postings given how many ask for German alongside English.
prose.getting_in: There's no license here, but 107 of the measured postings ask for a degree against 12 that waive it and 13 that call it preferred, so a bachelor's (often business or HR) is the norm rather than the exception. Experience requirements sit at a median of 4 years, though only 21 percent of postings state a number explicitly, which tells you a lot of employers are flexible if the rest of the profile fits. Employers who waive the degree usually accept a few years in a coordinator or sourcing role instead, proof you can run a pipeline without someone checking your work. The longest step is usually the first 18 months: getting from coordinator to full-cycle recruiter, since most companies won't hand you a req to own alone until you've sat through a full hiring season. German shows up in 141 of the language mentions against 49 for English, so in the Swiss and German market, language is often the real gate, not the degree.
prose.ladder: Early on you own candidates: sourcing, screening, keeping a pipeline moving. Mid-level, you start owning searches end to end, meaning you set the strategy with the hiring manager instead of just executing what they ask for. The next step up is owning a function or a region, which usually means less time on calls with candidates and more time managing other recruiters or building process (scorecards, interview training, comp benchmarking). That fork, individual contributor against people manager, tends to show up around the 4 to 6 year mark, and a fair number of good recruiters stay on the IC side deliberately because closing candidates is the part they're best at and don't want to give up.
prose.suits: People who do well here like the swing between structure and improvisation: you're running the same process every time but every candidate and every hiring manager is a different negotiation. If you get a charge out of talking someone into a role they weren't sure about, without pushing them into something wrong for them, this job gives you that most weeks. The people who leave are usually the ones who wanted to build things and found they were spending their days chasing feedback and rescheduling calls instead. If you need to see a finished product at the end of a project, the constant churn of the pipeline (roles close, then reopen six months later) can wear on you.
prose.misconceptions: People assume the job is mostly interviewing, when it's mostly sourcing and follow-up: finding the right 40 people to reach out to takes longer than talking to the 5 who respond. There's also an assumption that recruiters decide who gets hired. Mostly they decide who gets seen; the hiring manager decides who gets hired, and a recruiter's leverage is in shaping that shortlist and managing the process, not in the final call.
prose.who_qualifies: Supply chain analysts convert into this role at the highest measured rate (51 percent match), which tracks with how many of these postings are procurement-flavored recruiting rather than pure HR: sourcing suppliers and sourcing candidates use the same muscle. Customer support specialists (32 percent) already have the call volume and rejection tolerance built in. Lawyers show up at 30 percent too, likely from the same due-diligence, structured-interview instinct that recruiting rewards. What doesn't carry over cleanly from any of these is the sales instinct of closing a candidate on an offer they're wavering on; that's usually the part people have to build from scratch.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The postings can't tell you how much of the job is emotional labor, telling four strong candidates no in the same week you tell one yes. They also don't capture how much a bad hiring manager (vague, slow, or a moving target on requirements) can make an otherwise good search miserable, and how much of the job's difficulty depends on drawing a good one.

steps.do: Get a business or HR-adjacent degree
steps.how: A bachelor's is asked for in the large majority of postings that state an education requirement, typically business, HR, or psychology. This takes the standard 3 to 4 years, and if you're already past that stage, a few employers accept equivalent coordinator experience instead.

steps.do: Start as a recruiting or HR coordinator
steps.how: This is scheduling interviews, posting jobs, and doing first-pass resume screens for 12 to 18 months under someone else's searches. You're done with this step when you can run a full screen call alone and explain a rejection to a candidate without a script.

steps.do: Learn one applicant tracking system deeply
steps.how: Pick whatever your employer uses (often SAP-integrated in larger firms) and get fast at building boolean searches and pipeline reports in it. Two to three months of daily use is usually enough to stop feeling behind.

steps.do: Own a full search end to end
steps.how: Ask to run one requisition alone, from intake call with the hiring manager through offer, rather than just sourcing into someone else's search. This is the step that makes you a recruiter instead of a coordinator, and it usually happens somewhere in year 2.

steps.do: Add a language or a specialty
steps.how: In markets like Switzerland, German fluency alone changes which reqs you're trusted with (141 of the measured postings ask for it against 49 for English). Alternatively, go deep in one function, tech, finance, or executive search, which usually takes another year of focused searches in that area before you're the default person for it.

prose.tools: An applicant tracking system is the daily driver, and in larger or procurement-linked companies that's often SAP, which shows up in 7 percent of postings and tends to be a real gate for anyone targeting that segment. Excel comes up just as often for pipeline tracking and reporting. LinkedIn Recruiter and boolean search skills aren't listed as a named skill here but are assumed baseline for anyone doing sourcing. The tooling is drifting toward more structured data work: stakeholder management and data analysis both show up as named skills now, meaning recruiters are increasingly expected to report on pipeline health with numbers, not just gut feel.

industries.name: Procurement and manufacturing
industries.note: The largest segment by these postings, often blending recruiting with vendor and supply sourcing; SAP fluency matters more here than anywhere else.

industries.name: Corporate HR (tech, finance, professional services)
industries.note: Closest to the classic image of the role: full-cycle recruiting against internal headcount plans, less procurement crossover.

industries.name: Staffing agencies
industries.note: Faster pace, more searches running at once, and pay is often commission-linked to placements rather than salary alone.

industries.name: Public sector and NGOs
industries.note: Slower hiring cycles, more process and compliance around each hire, less pressure to close fast.

specializations.name: Technical recruiting
specializations.why: Companies hiring engineers pay a premium for recruiters who can evaluate a candidate's stack instead of relaying keywords, and the search cycles are longer and more competitive.

specializations.name: Executive search
specializations.why: Fewer, higher-stakes searches with much longer cycles and a heavier weight on discretion and relationship management; pay tops out well above the general median here.

specializations.name: Procurement-linked talent acquisition
specializations.why: Given how often SAP and procurement appear alongside recruiting in these postings, recruiters who can speak both languages (sourcing people and sourcing goods) are unusually well positioned in manufacturing-heavy markets like Switzerland and Germany.

pros: You get a concrete, immediate signal of success: an offer accepted, a start date confirmed, a seat filled.
The work rewards curiosity about people; every screen call is a short, structured conversation with someone new.
Skills transfer widely if you change your mind: the routes out include business analyst and management consulting roles, not just other HR jobs.
You build a genuinely large professional network almost by accident, just from years of screening calls.
cons: You spend real time chasing hiring managers for feedback that never comes on time, and that delay isn't yours to fix.
Rejecting strong candidates who did nothing wrong, just lost to someone else, happens weekly and doesn't get easier with volume.
Hiring freezes can kill a search you've spent a month on, with no warning and no do-over.
The job is judged almost entirely on speed and fill rate, which can push you to close a search before you're sure it's the right match.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a recruiter
faq.a: With a relevant bachelor's degree, most people spend 12 to 18 months as a coordinator before running their own full-cycle search. Without a degree, employers who waive it usually want a few years of coordinator or sourcing experience instead, so the timeline stretches but doesn't disappear.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a recruiter
faq.a: Not always: 12 of the measured postings explicitly waive the degree requirement, but 107 state one, so a bachelor's remains the norm. Employers who skip it are usually looking for proven coordinator or sourcing experience in its place.

faq.q: recruiter vs HR manager, what's the difference
faq.a: A recruiter owns the pipeline before someone's hired; an HR manager owns the employee after. The natural move from recruiter to HR manager shows up as the highest-matching route out at 36 percent, since the skills overlap heavily but the day-to-day (screening and closing versus performance and policy) doesn't.

Some can, but only 19 percent of these postings are remote, which is low compared to other business roles. The job leans on being reachable fast for both hiring managers and candidates, and a lot of the read on a candidate happens in real-time conversation, which pulls the role back toward the office.

faq.q: what does a recruiter get paid starting out versus later
faq.a: The lower quartile sits at $64k and the upper quartile at $135k, with the median at $91k, so the spread between someone early in coordinator-to-recruiter transition and someone running searches in a specialized or executive niche is wide. Language skills (German shows up far more than English in these postings) and sector, especially procurement-linked roles, shift where you land in that range.
